sections.label: Time to seek legal advice
sections.summary: The 14-day deadline applies only to filing the Notice for Leave to Appeal; after leave, the appellant has one month to file the Notice of Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked if it would be useful to give litigants-in-person more time beyond 14 days to seek legal advice to prepare the notice of appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: It is important to remember that the 14-day deadline is only for parties to file the Notice for Leave to Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: If the District Court gives leave to appeal, the appellant then has one month from that date to file his Notice of Appeal.

sections.label: Remitting cases to Tribunals
sections.summary: Clause 16 lets the District Court direct limited remittal to a differently constituted Tribunal, such as when new facts make the original decision manifestly unjust.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Clause 16 empowers the District Court to direct cases be remitted back to the Tribunals for reconsideration or rehearing by a differently constituted Tribunal only in limited cases, such as where new facts become available and it is manifestly unjust to allow the original decision to stand.

sections.label: Reviewing civil judgment enforcement
sections.summary: MinLaw is reviewing enforcement of civil judgments and orders, including Tribunal orders, to make enforcement more affordable and effective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Indeed, MinLaw is currently reviewing the process of enforcing civil judgments and orders and this includes orders by the Tribunals as well, with the aim of making the enforcement process more affordable and, as far as possible, more effective.

sections.label: Tribunals hearing tenancy claims
sections.summary: The Tribunals have heard tenancy claims involving unpaid rent since 2005 and developed expertise in such claims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: First, the Tribunals have been hearing tenancy claims involving unpaid rent for some time now since 2005, and they have developed the relevant expertise to deal with this type of claims.

sections.label: Guidelines for vacant possession orders
sections.summary: The State Courts will institute internal guidelines setting out factors the Tribunals consider before ordering delivery of vacant possession.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Third, to ensure safeguards, the State Courts will also be instituting internal guidelines which will set out the factors for the Tribunals to consider before making an order for the delivery of vacant possession.

sections.label: Tribunal claims from 2015 to 2017
sections.summary: From 2015 to 2017, the Tribunals handled an average of more than 10,000 claims annually.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: From 2015 to 2017, the Tribunals handled an average of more than 10,000 claims annually.

sections.label: State Courts claim case numbers
sections.summary: About 9,000 cases were filed in the State Courts with claims between $10,000 and $30,000 with consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Just as a ballpark indicator, the number of cases filed in the State Courts where the claim was between $10,000, the current limit, and $30,000, the new limit, with consent, is about 9,000.

sections.label: Clause 4 claim limit increase
sections.summary: Clause 4, read with clause 2, raises the limit to $20,000 by default, and to $30,000 by consent of all parties.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 4, read with clause 2 of the Bill, raises that limit to $20,000 by default, and that limit can also be increased by the consent of all the parties to $30,000.

sections.label: Tribunal amendments and claim limits
sections.summary: The amendments let Tribunals hear hire purchase claims under CPFTA, raise monetary limits and claim types, and extend the limitation period from one to two years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: With the amendments, the Tribunals will be able to hear hire purchase claims under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act (CPFTA).

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: In addition to raising the monetary limits of claims as well as the types of claims which can be filed, the proposed amendments will also extend the limitation period for lodging a claim in the Tribunals from one year to two years.

sections.label: Clause 20 consolidates Act provisions
sections.summary: Clause 20 consolidates different provisions in the Act to help people check if claims fall within its scope, except CPFTA claims under the Tribunals.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 20 of the Bill consolidates these different provisions within the framework of the Act to assist those wanting to find out whether their claims fall within the scope of the Act, with the only exception being the claims with regard to CPFTA which falls within the jurisdiction of the Tribunals.

sections.label: Clause 7 mandatory mediation power
sections.summary: Clause 7 empowers the Registrar or a tribunal to order parties to attend mandatory mediation at the Community Mediation Centre or before any other person.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: To address this situation, clause 7 of the Bill empowers the Registrar or a tribunal to order parties to attend mandatory mediation at the Community Mediation Centre, or before any other person.

sections.label: Clause 9 judge-led adjudication
sections.summary: Clause 9 requires a tribunal to adopt a judge-led approach at the Adjudication Stage.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 9 of the Bill requires a tribunal to adopt a judge-led approach at the Adjudication Stage.

sections.label: Renaming Referees as tribunal magistrates
sections.summary: Clause 3 renames the Referees as tribunal magistrates to reflect their roles and align with Employment Claims Tribunals nomenclature.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: To better reflect their roles and to align with the nomenclature used in the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT), clause 3 of the Bill renames the “Referees” as “tribunal magistrates”.

sections.label: District Court remitting cases back
sections.summary: Clause 16 provides that a District Court may remit a case back to the tribunal or order a rehearing by a different tribunal magistrate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 16 of the Bill now further refines this procedure by providing that a District Court may, even if it refuses leave to appeal, remit the case back to the tribunal for reconsideration, or order a rehearing presided by a different tribunal magistrate.

sections.label: Tribunals caseload statistics
sections.summary: The Tribunals disposed of about 39,000 cases in 1998 and 1999, with 10,908 in 2015, 10,266 in 2016 and a projected 9,700 in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Starting out with a caseload of about 3,000, the Tribunals disposed of approximately 39,000 cases in 1998 and 1999.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the most recent statistics available, the numbers were 10,908 in 2015; 10,266 in 2016; and a projected 9,700 in 2017.

sections.label: Raising monetary claim thresholds
sections.summary: The threshold was $2,000 in 1984, raised to $5,000 in 1995, then $10,000 with consent, and $10,000 and $20,000 with consent in 1997.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In 1984, the threshold was $2,000, with the rationale that resolving such claims through the normal civil Courts may be seen to be costly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It was raised in 1995 to $5,000 and then $10,000 with consent; and, subsequently, to $10,000 and $20,000 with consent in 1997.

sections.label: Extending limitation period
sections.summary: Another expansion of jurisdiction is the extension of the limitation period from one to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Yet another expansion of jurisdiction is the extension of the limitation period from one to two years.

sections.label: Workers' Party supports Bill amendments
sections.summary: The Workers' Party supports the Bill, which raises the default monetary limit to $20,000 and the upper limit to $30,000 with consent, and expands subject-matter jurisdiction to hire purchase claims under CPFTA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Workers’ Party supports the proposed amendments in this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This Bill proposes, first, to raise the default monetary limit of the Tribunals to $20,000, and the upper limit to $30,000 with the consent of all parties to a dispute.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Bill also proposes to expand the Tribunals' subject-matter jurisdiction to include hire purchase claims under CPFTA.

sections.label: Tribunal magistrates capacity and time bar
sections.summary: Asks about expected increase in tribunal magistrates and when capacity increases will occur, and notes the Bill proposes raising the time bar from one to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Two, what, if any, is the expected increase in the number of tribunal magistrates to deal with any increase in the caseload, and when will the capacity increase for tribunal magistrates as well as administrative staff be put in place?

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Next, the Bill also proposes to increase the time bar for claims under the Tribunals from one to two years.

sections.label: Support for higher limits and limitation period
sections.summary: Supports raising the Tribunals' monetary limits and extending the limitation period from one year to two years for claimants.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Raising of the monetary limits of the Tribunals’ jurisdiction will be a boon for claimants and freelance workers alike as I know of professional freelancers who take their clients to task at the Tribunals for non-payment of work done under their contracts for service.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: I am also supportive of the extension of the limitation period for cases to be brought to the Tribunals as members of the public who are not familiar with legal processes may not consider legal recourse until the dispute has remained unresolved for some time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: It is thus reasonable to extend the limitation period from one year to two years for the claimants to avail themselves of the opportunity to bring their small claims to the Tribunals.

sections.label: Enforcement of tribunal orders
sections.summary: Asks how many of the 9,700 cases in 2017 had orders fully satisfied and whether enforcement success rates differ from the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: According to the State Courts Annual Report 2017, 9,700 cases came before the Tribunals in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Of these cases, how many orders were fully satisfied?

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Does the success rate of enforcement of tribunal orders differ from that of judgments made by the Courts?

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: In the same way that processes to access the Tribunals have to be simplified so that end users are able to obtain the best substantive as well as procedural justice available, the process to seek enforcement of tribunal judgments should also be simplified and made more accessible so that enforcement arrangements do not impact the efficiency of the small claims procedure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: To mitigate this issue, the Tribunals can do more by better informing claimants of the potential problems of enforcement, incorporate processes to filter out claims which should not be pursued because of the poor chance of collection and explore ways to better ensure efficient enforcement of its orders, given the nature of the Tribunals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: First, from the workers’ point of view, freelancers and the self-employed people will be able to claim a higher amount, hence, there is better protection for them.

sections.label: Increase in monetary limits
sections.summary: States that increasing limits from $20,000 to $30,000, compared to the current $10,000 to $20,000, will be well received by consumers.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Increasing limits from $20,000 to $30,000, compared to the current $10,000 to $20,000 respectively, will be well received by consumers.

sections.label: Flexible compensation and renaming Referee
sections.summary: Says giving the Tribunals flexibility to order non-monetary compensation is a step in a right direction and renaming Referee to Tribunal Magistrate confers authority and respect.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Giving the Tribunals more flexibility to order other forms of compensation and not just monetary order is a step in a right direction so as to allow more equitable compensation of varied forms.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Renaming “Referee” to Tribunal Magistrate confers the judge the authority and respect that should be accorded in facilitating the tribunal process.

sections.label: Class action under sections 26 and 27
sections.summary: Asks whether class action can be taken in cases like o-Bike if the combined value of claims heard together does not exceed the Tribunals' monetary jurisdiction.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under sections 26 and 27, with regard to cases like o-Bike, can class action be taken if the case satisfies the criterion that the combined value of the claims heard together does not exceed the Tribunals' monetary jurisdiction?

sections.label: Consent limit raised to $30,000
sections.summary: Where both parties consent, the default limit is raised from $20,000 to $30,000.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: In situations where there is mutual consent by both parties, the default will be raised from $20,000 to $30,000.

sections.label: Limitation period raised to two years
sections.summary: The limitation period for disputes brought to the Tribunal is raised from one year to two years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The limitation period for disputes to be brought to the Tribunal is also raised from one year to two years.

sections.label: Cooling off period for elderly consumers
sections.summary: A Member asks for a two-week cooling off period, like insurance products, to be implemented and enforced by the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Even when prices are stated clearly, the elderly sometimes fail to notice the small print or they simply get confused by all the different numbers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: I hope a two-week cooling off period, like that for insurance products, can be implemented and enforced by the Government.

sections.label: Judge-led Tribunal proceedings and mediation
sections.summary: The Tribunals will adopt a judge-led approach and parties may attend mediation, with costs awarded where appropriate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The Tribunals will adopt a judge-led approach during Tribunal proceedings or the parties to attend mediation and costs awarded against parties where appropriate.

sections.label: Mandatory hire purchase dispute clause
sections.summary: A Member asks if the Minister would consider making it mandatory for hire purchase contracts to include a clause allowing parties to turn to the Tribunals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: For the consumers to be able to turn to the Tribunal, this would help save them much time and it will probably be more cost-effective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It is, indeed, good that the limitation period is raised from one year to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Given that there is now this amendment to the Act, may I ask if the Minister would consider making it mandatory for all hire purchase contracts to include a clause that says something to the effect that in the event of a dispute or disagreement within the period of two years, both parties may turn to the Tribunals to resolve any dispute?

sections.label: Disputes in third year and raised limits
sections.summary: A Member asks whether parties could turn to the Tribunal in the third year, and welcomes raised monetary limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Can I ask in this instance if there is a dispute under such a contract during the third year, could the parties be allowed to turn to the Tribunal for resolution?

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: After all, the initial contract signed was for a two-year period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I am also pleased that the monetary limits have been increased from $10,000 to $20,000 and the extended limit subject to both parties’ concurrence is raised from $20,000 to 30,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Small Claims Tribunal (Amendment) Bill introduces various amendments to the Act aimed to expand and enhance both the jurisdiction and powers of the Tribunals.

sections.label: Clauses 12 and 13 amendments
sections.summary: Clauses 12 and 13 amend sections to clarify that aggregate value of class action or consolidated claims does not exceed the Act's monetary limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Clauses 12 and 13 of the Bill amends these sections to clarify that the aggregate value of the class action or consolidated claims does not exceed the monetary limits prescribed by the Act.

sections.label: Tribunals power to order costs
sections.summary: The proposed amendment aims to give Tribunals power to order a party to pay costs where the Tribunal thinks fit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In particular, the proposed amendment aims to provide the Tribunals the power to order a party to pay costs where the Tribunal thinks fit to do so.

sections.label: New section 35 vacant possession
sections.summary: Proposed new section 35 empowers Tribunals to order vacant possession of premises in cases involving unpaid rent by a tenant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The proposed new section 35 of the Act will also now empower the Tribunals to order vacant possession of the premises in cases involving unpaid rent by a tenant.

sections.label: Clause 16 appeal amendments
sections.summary: Clause 16 amends section 38 to let the District Court, when leave to appeal is refused, remit the matter back or order a rehearing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Third, section 38 of the present Act provides that there will be no appeal to the High Court against the Tribunal’s decision unless it involves a question of law or jurisdiction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Clause 16 of the Bill proposes to amend this section to allow the District Court to, in cases where leave to appeal is refused, order that the matter be remitted back to the same tribunal for reconsideration or that the case be reheard by a different tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It appears that the effect of the proposed amendments is to give the District Court supervisory jurisdiction over the Tribunals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: However, this seems to be inconsistent with section 19(3) of the State Courts Act, which explicitly states that the District Court does not have any supervisory jurisdiction.

sections.label: Clarification on appeal scope
sections.summary: The member asks the Senior Minister of State to clarify if the approach has changed and why the scope for appeal needs expanding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Could the hon Senior Minister of State please clarify if the approach has changed and, if so, why is there a need to expand the scope for appeal?

sections.label: Registrar referring claims to mediation
sections.summary: The member supports the Registrar's power under section 18A to refer a claim for mediation, with cases automatically referred unless parties opt out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As mentioned, I am very supportive of the Registrar now having the power to refer a claim for mediation under section 18A.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There is a presumption of alternative dispute resolution for all civil cases under the State Court Practice Directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Court will automatically refer all cases to the most appropriate mode of alternative dispute resolution, including mediation, unless parties opt out.

sections.label: Cost of enforcing money order
sections.summary: Minister Shanmugam estimated enforcing a Tribunal money order costs between $400 and $600, about a quarter of the $2,000 claim limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, in a written response to a 2017 Parliamentary Question, Minister Shanmugam estimated the total cost of enforcing a money order of the Tribunal can be between $400 and $600.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This is about a quarter of the claim limit of $2,000 before the Tribunal.

sections.label: Increase in jurisdictional limit
sections.summary: The amendments propose raising the jurisdictional limit to S$20,000 by default and up to S$30,000 if parties agree.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The amendments propose an increase in the quantum of jurisdictional limit to S$20,000, by default, and up to S$30,000 if parties agree to the same.

sections.label: Limitation period and claim types
sections.summary: The limitation period rises from one to two years, and the amendments broaden claim types to include hire purchase claims and others.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The limitation period for bringing a claim to the Tribunals has also been increased from one year to two years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Additionally, the amendments also seek to broaden the types of claims that can be heard at the Tribunals, such as hire purchase claims, in addition to pre-existing categories, such as any contract for sale of goods or provision of services; claim in tort in respect of any property; and contract for the lease of residential premises that does not exceed two years.

sections.label: District Courts remit matters
sections.summary: District Courts would be empowered to remit a matter to the Tribunal for reconsideration, order a rehearing, and grant a stay of execution.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In this regard, I am happy to note that District Courts would be empowered to remit a matter to the Tribunal for reconsideration or order a rehearing by a different tribunal and grant a stay of execution where appropriate.

sections.label: CJTS filing and call centre
sections.summary: Since 10 July 2017 the CJTS lets parties file claims from home, supported by a call centre handling procedural calls.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Since 10 July 2017, the CJTS allows for parties to file claims from the comfort of their homes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: It is also important for this system to be supported by a call centre where calls about procedure are dealt with.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I believe this is similar to the suggestion by fellow Member Ms Joan Pereira.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: These calls can be managed by a trained pool of paralegals who may be the best placed to assist.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: At the Tribunals, we must continue to remain open to assist those in need of guidance, keeping in mind that such officers can render legal advice.

sections.label: CASE supports jurisdiction extension
sections.summary: CASE supports extending the Tribunal's jurisdiction to $20,000, the extended limit to $30,000, and the limitation period to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: And that is the thrust of what a Tribunal is about.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: Hence, CASE supports the extension of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to $20,000 and the prescribed extended limit is increased to $30,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: CASE is also supportive of the increase in the limitation period from one year to two years.

sections.label: o-Bike rental deposit refunds
sections.summary: Consumers sought refunds of o-Bike rental deposits at the Tribunals, but section 5 of the SCT Act does not provide for such claims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: Recently, when o-Bike announced that they were ceasing to operate in Singapore, many consumers wanted to submit their claims to the Tribunals to ask for the refund of the rental deposits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: However, section 5 of the SCT Act does not provide for claims for refund of rental deposits.

sections.label: Unfair Contract Terms Act amendment
sections.summary: The Member urges the Minister to insert a clause amending the Act so businesses cannot oust Tribunal jurisdiction by referring disputes to arbitration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: The Unfair Contracts Terms Act would also have no meaning as businesses which impose unfair contractual terms can assert that "businesses are free to enter into consumer contracts, as long as it is mutually agreed to by the contracting parties".

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: Hence, I urge the Minister to consider inserting a new clause to amend the Act, which should not allow businesses to oust the jurisdiction of the Tribunal by referring disputes within the specified limit for arbitration.

sections.label: Small Claims Tribunals Bill enhancements
sections.summary: The Member says it is an opportune moment to enhance the Small Claims Tribunals Bill and will raise three points.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Certainly, it is an opportune moment to introduce some enhancements to the Small Claims Tribunals Bill.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I will raise three points today: preventing abuse of the mediation process, legal representation for individuals, and public education.

sections.label: Community Mediation Centre time limits
sections.summary: The Member asks how the Ministry will prevent this and whether the CMC will limit mediation to one day like Magistrate-referred cases.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: How will the Ministry ensure that this does not happen?

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Community Mediation Centre (CMC) limit the mediation to one day, just like it does for Magistrate-referred cases?

sections.label: Legal representation during Tribunal mediation
sections.summary: The Member asks whether a layman can be allowed legal representation during Small Claims Tribunal Mediation.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: To better address the imbalance of bargaining power and prevent issues arising from the individual not understanding his or her legal rights, can layman be allowed legal representation during Small Claims Tribunal Mediation?

sections.label: Freelancers using the Tribunal
sections.summary: Freelancers lack Employment Act security and use the Tribunal for unpaid services, so higher claim values and judge-led proceedings will help them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: They do not have the security provided by the Employment Act and some use the Tribunal as a main recourse to pursue unpaid services or when disputes in the provision of services occur.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Therefore, the increase in monetary value of claims and the adoption of judge-led proceedings will help the freelancers.

sections.label: Cost of enforcing Tribunal claims
sections.summary: Filing claims costs 1% of the claim amount for consumers, but enforcement costs may reach $400 to $600 if a writ of seizure is needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: While the cost of filing claims in the Tribunals is affordable, at 1% of the claim amount for consumers, this cost quickly escalates in the enforcement of the claims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Should the other party resist compliance, a writ of seizure may need to be issued and the administrative and ancillary costs may come up to $400 to $600 easily.

sections.label: Barrier for people without legal background
sections.summary: The speaker asks MinLaw to simplify the claims process, reduce legal jargon and streamline enforcement of Court judgments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: For people without any legal background, this is obviously a major barrier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: I hope MinLaw can continue to simplify the claims process and reduce legal jargons, in particular, the process of enforcing the Court judgment should be streamlined.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunals' coverage of new areas
sections.summary: The Ministry will monitor developments in new areas and review their suitability for inclusion in the Tribunals' coverage later.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Nonetheless, we assure Members that my Ministry will closely monitor these developments in these new areas and continue to review their suitability for inclusion within the Tribunals' coverage at a later stage.

sections.label: Slow to mandate contract clauses
sections.summary: Heavy-handed intervention could distort markets, so the Government is slow to mandate clauses and has not introduced cooling-off periods for hire purchase contracts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: A too heavy-handed intervention in favour of either party could lead to market distortions or unintended consequences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Hence, we wish to be slow to mandate the use of specific clauses in commercial contracts between private individuals and businesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Likewise, this is why the Government has not introduced cooling-off periods for hire purchase contracts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As Mr Lim Biow Chuan, President of CASE, correctly pointed out, contractual terms which are substantively unfair, based on widespread international consensus, can still be voided under the Unfair Contract Terms Act (UCTA).

sections.label: Tripartite Standard on Contracting with Self-Employed
sections.summary: The Tripartite Standard on Contracting with Self-Employed Persons, guidelines on engaging freelance services, was launched in March 2018 with Government support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For example, the Tripartite Standard on Contracting with Self-Employed Persons, a set of guidelines on best practices for engaging freelance services, was launched in March 2018 with the support of the Government.

sections.label: Pre-filing assessment and e-Negotiation outcomes
sections.summary: Some claimants said pre-filing assessment and notifications helped them understand jurisdiction and issues; e-Negotiation was used in 755 cases, with about one-third settling online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Our experience so far has been to the contrary, as some claimants have commented that the pre-filing assessment and list of notifications, in fact, helped them better understand the jurisdiction of the Tribunals, and see in advance the potential issues of their case so that they are better prepared.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Between 10 July 2017 and 15 June 2018, e-Negotiation has been used by parties in 755 cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In about one-third of those cases, parties reached a settlement online.

sections.label: Lodgement fees for claims
sections.summary: Lodgement fees for consumer claims range from $10 to $200, and for non-consumer claims from $50 to $600 or 3% of the amount.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Today, lodgement fees for consumer claims range from $10 for claims up to $5,000 in value, or up to $200 for the maximum limit of a $20,000 claim.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For non-consumer claims, the lodgement fees range from $50 for claims up to $5,000, or to $600 for claims up to $20,000, or 3% of the amount in question.

sections.label: Tribunals ordering costs
sections.summary: The amendments allow the Tribunals to order costs at their discretion in the most egregious cases of abusive conduct.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This has limited the Tribunals’ ability to manage litigants who conduct their cases in an abusive manner.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Thus, the amendments allow the Tribunals to order costs at their discretion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The intention is for such cost orders to be made only in the most egregious of cases, where a party has been unusually disruptive, uncooperative or contemptuous, even if the claim itself cannot be said to be frivolous.

sections.label: Mediation and amicable settlement
sections.summary: The proposed amendments empower the Registrar or Tribunals to order parties to attend mediation at the CMC or before another person.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Even if there is a dispute, one should not rule out an amicable settlement even at a late stage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I mentioned earlier that the proposed amendments to empower the Registrar or the Tribunals to order parties to attend mediation at the CMC or before any other person.

sections.label: Unreasonable refusal to mediate
sections.summary: If a party is wholly unreasonable in refusing to mediate or disruptive during mediation, the Tribunals can take this into account when deciding costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: If, however, a party is wholly unreasonable in refusing to mediate, is unusually disruptive or is very uncooperative or takes a very unreasonably disruptive stance during mediation, then the Tribunals can and should take this into account when deciding on costs at the end of the day.

sections.label: Monitoring and next review
sections.summary: The need or demand for such actions will continue to be monitored, and Mr Murali Pillai's suggestion of an intermediate solution considered in the next review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Nonetheless, we will continue to monitor the need or demand for such actions, and also consider Mr Murali Pillai's suggestion of an "intermediate solution" of stipulating a higher monetary limit for the aggregate value of consolidated or representative claims in our next review.

sections.label: Claims without documentary evidence
sections.summary: Ms Joan Pereira asked how claimants can establish their claims in the Tribunals where documentary evidence is not available.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Ms Joan Pereira asked how claimants can establish their claims in the Tribunals where documentary evidence is not available.

sections.label: Tribunals evidence and stamp duty
sections.summary: The Tribunals would consider evidence such as oral representations and whether goods were satisfactory, and Ms Joan Pereira asked if a landlord may recover stamp duty as damages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Tribunals would also look at, for instance, evidence as to whether the seller, for example, had made an oral representation, and what those terms of the oral representation might be, whether or not the goods that were sold were objectively of a satisfactory and acceptable state or otherwise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Relatedly, Ms Joan Pereira asked whether, where the tenant breaches the tenancy contract, the landlord may recover the stamp duty paid as damages.
